definition: A diaspora is a people scattered far from their homeland — and the name for the scattered community itself, settled in many countries yet still one people.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word diaspora. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know diaspora should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Letters, remittances, and recipes stitched the island's diaspora to villages its children had never seen.
Migration is milder than diaspora: a migrating people may move once and settle together in a single new home, while a diaspora is flung across many countries at once, with the homeland left behind.

Dissolution goes further than diaspora — a diaspora is scattered yet still one people, writing home and marrying in, while dissolution means the scattering wins and the community quietly stops being a community at all.

Dispersion is the physics-neutral word for things spread out from a center — seeds, droplets, data points. Diaspora is dispersion with a people and a homeland in it: the scattered still belong to somewhere, and to each other.

An exodus is the mass departure itself — one dramatic leaving, out the door together. A diaspora is what exists afterward and for generations: the same people, now settled in many places, still tied to the home they left.

The word asks for a whole people dispersed from a shared homeland, and for the threads that keep the scattered community one thing: the reunions, the pattern books, the sense that 'home' still names the valley.
formal / historical and cultural
Diaspora began as a proper noun — the Diaspora, the Jewish communities living outside Judea — and the capital-D sense is still current.
Lowercase, it now serves any people scattered from a homeland: writers speak of the Irish, Armenian, or West African diaspora.
It is a collective word; one emigrant belongs to a diaspora but cannot be one.
And mind the timeline it implies: an exodus is the departure itself, the event — a diaspora is the long afterward, measured in generations.
